title: Syllabus
text:
Course description
Project management as it is actually practiced: the quantitative core (work breakdown, critical path method, PERT, earned value management) alongside adaptive delivery (Scrum, Kanban, flow metrics), with hybrid approaches treated as the default real-world case rather than a compromise. The course argues from empirical evidence rather than from convention — students learn to distinguish a base rate from a vendor statistic and to say what a project-success number is actually measuring.
Running through every week is an AI layer. Students progress from grounded prompting, through model-generated artifacts verified by code they write themselves, to specifying and building agents that maintain live project artifacts — and to governing those agents, which is the project-management problem the textbooks have not caught up with yet.

title: Syllabus
text:
Course objectives
By the end of the course a student can:

Decide which delivery approach fits a given project and defend the choice against a specific alternative.
Build and interpret the core quantitative artifacts: WBS, CPM network, PERT distribution, crash analysis, EVM report.
Run the adaptive artifacts: product backlog, sprint mechanics, cumulative flow diagram, Little’s Law.
Read the evidence critically — distinguish a base rate from a vendor statistic.
Diagnose a failing project and propose interventions ranked by expected effect, not by convention.
Specify, build, and govern an AI agent that maintains a live project artifact, and state what it got wrong.


Additional expectations for students enrolled in IMSE 656
Students enrolled under the graduate number complete the same components at a higher level of expectation:

Conceptual assignments include an additional short-answer section requiring students to ground a claim in one of the primary sources on the source shelf.
Final project must include a methods justification section: the choice of delivery approach, estimating method, and control mechanism defended against the empirical literature, with citations.
Final presentation includes a five-minute defence against a challenge from the instructor drawn from the counter-evidence for the position taken.

title: Syllabus
text:
Artificial intelligence policy
AI use is expected, not merely permitted. Much of this course is about using these tools well. Three rules make that workable:

Label it. Any submitted artifact that an AI system produced or substantially drafted says so, names the tool, and includes the prompt or a link to the conversation.
Verify it. Every quantitative result generated by a model must be accompanied by the code or hand calculation that checks it. A number you cannot verify is a number you did not produce. This is graded.
Own it. You are responsible for everything you submit, including the parts a model wrote. “The AI said so” is not a defence, in this course or in a project review.

The midterm is the exception: it is closed-book, closed-notes, and computer-free, because the reasoning it tests is the reasoning you need when the tool is unavailable or wrong.

text:
What this course deliberately does not cover
Stating exclusions explicitly is more useful than pretending to comprehensiveness:

PMP exam drilling. The exam changes; the reasoning does not. The credential is mentioned, not taught to.
Tool tutorials (MS Project, Jira, Primavera). One is assigned as homework infrastructure; no lecture time goes to menus.
The full process catalogue of PMBOK 8. You learn the shape of a process standard and how to look things up. Memorizing inputs-tools-outputs is the lowest-value activity in project-management education.
Scaling frameworks in depth (SAFe, LeSS, Nexus). One segment on why they exist and why the evidence for them is thin.
Six Sigma and lean manufacturing. Adjacent field, separate course.
Contract law. Contract types and incentive structure are covered; the law is not.

title: Week 13 — People, stakeholders, and governance
text:
Attack this claim

“Project success depends primarily on the competence of the project manager.”

Attack with Young & Jordan directly: the evidence points above the PM. But then attack that — the studies are cross-sectional, self-reported, and mostly IS/IT; Blaskovics’s 3,153-project LASSO puts PM competence first. Have students identify the actual disagreement (unit of analysis, project type, and how “support” was operationalized) rather than picking a side.

title: Week 13 — People, stakeholders, and governance
text:
Somewhere else entirely
A film director’s relationship with a studio. The director has enormous creative authority and almost no financial authority. Films die because the studio stopped believing in them, not because the director lost competence. Ask students what a director does about that — and notice that the answer is politics, relationships, and early visible wins, which is exactly what the CSF literature keeps finding.

title: Week 11 — Adaptive delivery — Scrum, Kanban, flow
text:
The evidence

Serrador & Pinto (2015), 1,002 projects: agile use positively affected both efficiency and overall stakeholder satisfaction; quality of the project vision/goals was a marginally significant moderator.
Koch et al. (2023), pre-registered meta-analysis, k = 41, N = 73,825: small effects on job satisfaction, strain, and commitment; medium-to-large effects on performance and innovative behaviour; medium effect on psychological empowerment. Effects were stronger outside software (manufacturing, healthcare, logistics) and stronger in published than unpublished records — note the publication-bias signal to students.
Lieberum et al. (2022), M&SOM, controlled lab experiment with a 2×2 design: performance was higher with time-boxed progression, because under flexible progression people over-invest in early phases — the “progression fallacy.” Adding self-imposed phase goals on top of time-boxing added nothing; combining phase goals with flexible progression (i.e. traditional PM) made things actively worse. This is the cleanest causal evidence available that the timebox specifically is doing work.
Contra: Badran et al. (2024), 392 construction project managers in Jordan: agile PM positively affected innovation, responsiveness, quality and client satisfaction but negatively affected cost performance and had no significant effect on time. Domain matters.

title: Week 11 — Adaptive delivery — Scrum, Kanban, flow
text:
Check yourself

Who is accountable for the Product Backlog? Can a committee hold that accountability?
What is the commitment attached to the Increment, and what happens if the team redefines it mid-sprint?
Our team has 30 items in progress and finishes 5 per week. A stakeholder wants to know when their new item will be done. What do you tell them, and what should you change?
What does Scrum say about budgets, contracts, or portfolios? Why is that silence deliberate?

title: Week 11 — Adaptive delivery — Scrum, Kanban, flow
text:
Attack this claim

“Agile is better than waterfall.”

Force decomposition: better at which success dimension, in which domain, measured how? The honest synthesis: strong evidence for stakeholder and team dimensions, mixed-to-weak for cost, domain-dependent throughout, and much of the primary evidence is self-reported survey data with obvious selection effects.

title: Week 11 — Adaptive delivery — Scrum, Kanban, flow
text:
Somewhere else entirely
Jazz ensemble vs. symphony orchestra. The orchestra has a score (baseline), a conductor (PM), and rehearsals that converge on a fixed performance. The jazz quartet has a head (product goal), agreed changes (definition of done), and improvises within them. Neither is better. But note: the quartet’s freedom depends on every member being individually excellent, which is precisely the condition organizations skip when they “adopt agile.”

title: Week 9 — Earned Value Management
text:
Worked example
Project: BAC = $500,000, planned duration 20 weeks. At end of week 8: PV = $200,000, EV = $170,000, AC = $190,000.

CV = 170,000 − 190,000 = −$20,000 (over cost)
SV = 170,000 − 200,000 = −$30,000 (behind schedule)
CPI = 170/190 = 0.895 → getting 89.5 cents of value per dollar
SPI = 170/200 = 0.850
EAC (typical) = 500,000/0.8947 = $558,824
EAC (atypical) = 190,000 + 330,000 = $520,000
EAC (both indices) = 190,000 + 330,000/(0.8947 × 0.85) = $623,910
ETC (typical) = 558,824 − 190,000 = $368,824
VAC = 500,000 − 558,824 = −$58,824
TCPI(BAC) = 330,000/310,000 = 1.065 → you now need 6.5% better than planned efficiency for the rest of the project, having averaged 10.5% worse. Ask the class whether that’s plausible. It almost never is, and that is the single most useful thing EVM tells a manager.

The spread between $520k and $624k is the lesson. The formula choice is a judgement about causation, not a computation. Make students defend a choice.
The SPI pathology. As a project approaches completion, EV → BAC and PV → BAC, so SPI → 1 regardless of how late the project is. A project delivering a year late shows SPI = 1.00 on its final day. SPI is also denominated in dollars, not time.
Earned Schedule fixes this. ES = the time at which the planned value equals the current earned value: find t such that PV(t) = EV. Then SPI(t) = ES/AT, and IEAC(t) = PD/SPI(t).
Continuing the example with PV accruing linearly at $25,000/week: ES = 170,000/25,000 = 6.80 weeks. AT = 8. SPI(t) = 6.80/8 = 0.850. IEAC(t) = 20/0.85 = 23.5 weeks — a forecast in time units, which SPI cannot give you. (With a linear PV curve SPI and SPI(t) coincide; with a realistic S-curve they diverge, and they diverge most near the end, which is exactly where you need the number.)
Does EVM actually forecast well? Yes, with caveats, and the evidence is decent. Batselier & Vanhoucke (2015, JCEM) evaluated EVM forecasting on 51 real projects (mostly construction) plus Monte Carlo support and found that highly accurate time and cost forecasts are obtainable, while identifying which methods perform best. Barrientos-Orellana et al. (2021, 2023) compared 27 duration and 30 cost methods across 4,100 simulated networks and found the simplest formulations were most stable and accurate, with accuracy degrading as networks become more parallel. De Marco et al. (2023, 79 projects) report EAC MAPE improving from ~14.6% early to ~11.4% late under a proactive risk strategy.
What EVM cannot see: quality, stakeholder satisfaction, whether the scope was worth building, rework not yet discovered, and any risk that hasn’t yet hit the ledger. A project can show CPI = 1.0 the week before it is cancelled.

title: Week 9 — Earned Value Management

Attack this claim

“EVM gives objective, quantitative project control.”

Attack: EV depends on a subjective percent-complete judgement (0/100, 50/50, and level-of-effort rules all produce different EVs from the same work); the baseline is a forecast, so EVM measures deviation from a guess; it is silent on quality and value; and it can be gamed by claiming credit early.

Check yourself

PMBOK went from 49 processes → 0 → 40 in eight years. What problem was each swing solving?
Which of these four documents could you actually sue someone over? Why does that matter?

title: Week 2 — The standards landscape, and how to read a standard
text:
Attack this claim

“Standards bodies revise their frameworks primarily to sell new certifications, not because knowledge advanced.”

This one is uncomfortable and partly defensible — make students separate the cynical claim (revenue motive) from the testable one (did practice improve?). Note that the Scrum Guide, which is free and unrevised for six years, is the counterexample that complicates the cynical reading.

title: Week 2 — The standards landscape, and how to read a standard
text:
Somewhere else entirely
Building codes vs. architectural style. A building code is prescriptive, legally enforceable, and says nothing about whether the building is good. A style is a set of principles a designer can violate deliberately. PRINCE2 is closer to a code; PMBOK 7/8 is closer to a style guide; Scrum is closer to a poetic form — a sonnet is 14 lines, and the constraint is the point.

title: IMSE 456/656 — Project Management
text: Project management taught the way it is actually practiced now: the quantitative core (WBS, CPM, PERT, EVM) alongside adaptive delivery (Scrum, Kanban, flow), with hybrid treated as the default real-world case rather than a compromise — and with an AI layer running through every week, because the artifacts of this discipline are increasingly drafted by machines and audited by people.

title: IMSE 456/656 — Project Management
section: What you will be able to do
text:
What you will be able to do

Decide which delivery approach fits a given project and defend the choice against a specific alternative.
Build and interpret the core quantitative artifacts: WBS, CPM network, PERT distribution, crash analysis, EVM report.
Run the adaptive artifacts: product backlog, sprint mechanics, cumulative flow, Little’s Law.
Read the evidence critically — distinguish a base rate from a vendor statistic, and name what a project-success number is actually measuring.
Diagnose a failing project and propose interventions ranked by expected effect, not by convention.
Specify, build, and govern an AI agent that maintains a live project artifact — and say what it got wrong.

title: AI Studio
text:
Project management is one of the first disciplines where the routine artifacts — charters, work breakdowns, risk registers, status reports — can be drafted by a machine in seconds. That does not make the discipline easier. It moves the difficulty from production to judgement: someone still has to know whether the WBS is complete, whether the estimate is defensible, and whether the status report is telling the truth.
This course teaches that judgement by making you use the tools constantly and hold them to account every time.

title: AI Studio
text:
The ALTER system
Five roles, five different jobs. The framework is Sandeep Swadia’s “University in a Box” from How To Become Dangerously Self-Educated (with AI); every week’s notes carry all five.








Role
Its job
Where you meet it




Adviser
Sets destination, baseline, sequencing, cut list
The syllabus — including what this course deliberately does not cover


Librarian
Curates credible sources, defends against distraction
The source shelf below, and per-week readings


Tutor
Asks one question at a time, finds the gap, does not lecture
“Tutor check” in every week’s notes; the per-week prompts in each lab


Editor
Challenges logic, finds weak arguments, cuts repetition
“Editor challenge” — a defensible-sounding claim you have to attack


Roommate
Brings perspective from an unrelated field
“Roommate link” — a cross-domain analogy that transfers structure, not vocabulary




Tutor
Be my tutor on [TOPIC] in project management. Ask me one question at a
time. Don't lecture me. Find the gap in my understanding. Be precise.

When I get something wrong, don't correct me immediately — ask a follow-up
that makes me find the error myself. Only explain after I've tried twice.

Two commands I'll use: "teach me" means give me the explanation now; "test
me" means switch to harder questions on the same topic.
For exam preparation, the retrieval variant — mixed questions drawn from all prior weeks, not the current one. Mixing is what makes retrieval practice work.


Editor
Attack what I just wrote. Find the weakest link in the argument, the claim
that isn't supported, and the place where I've confused a definition with
a conclusion. Be specific and be harsh. Don't tell me what's good about it.


Roommate
I've just learned [CONCEPT] in project management. You work in a completely
different field. Where does this same structure show up in your world, and
what does your version know that mine doesn't?

title: AI Studio
text:
The source shelf
Everything else is optional reading. Load these into a single grounded workspace and make the assistant answer from the shelf, not from the open web.
Standards — look at them; do not memorize them.

PMI, A Guide to the Project Management Body of Knowledge (PMBOK Guide) — Eighth Edition, November 2025 — https://www.pmi.org/standards/pmbok
Schwaber & Sutherland, The Scrum Guide, November 2020 — https://scrumguides.org
Beck et al., Manifesto for Agile Software Development, 2001 — https://agilemanifesto.org
ISO 21502:2020, Project, programme and portfolio management — Guidance on project management

Empirical anchors — the papers this course actually argues from.

Gemino, Horner Reich & Serrador (2021), “Agile, Traditional, and Hybrid Approaches to Project Success”, Project Management Journal. 477 projects.
Serrador & Pinto (2015), “Does Agile work? — A quantitative analysis of agile project success”, IJPM. 1,002 projects.
Koch et al. (2023), “The affective, behavioural and cognitive outcomes of agile project management: A preliminary meta-analysis”, JOOP. Pre-registered; k = 41, N = 73,825.
Young & Jordan (2008), “Top management support: mantra or necessity?”; Young & Poon (2013), IJPM.
Batselier & Vanhoucke (2015), “Empirical Evaluation of Earned Value Management Forecasting Accuracy”, JCEM. 51 real projects.
Flyvbjerg (2021), “Top Ten Behavioral Biases in Project Management”, PMJ. Base rates from 2,062 projects.
Love, Ika et al. (2019), “The cost performance of transportation projects: The fallacy of the Planning Fallacy account”, TR Part A. The counter-case.
Eveleens & Verhoef (2010), “The Rise and Fall of the Chaos Report Figures”, IEEE Software 27(1):30–36.







The two failure modes



The model agrees with you. Every prompt above is written to make the assistant adversarial, because the default behaviour is accommodation. If your Editor pass comes back mostly positive, the prompt didn’t take — re-run it with “you were too generous; find three more problems and be harsher.”
The model invents a citation. Ask for a source and you will often get a plausible-looking one that does not exist, or a real paper with the wrong finding attached. Anything you are going to put in a report, verify against the actual document. This is the entire reason the Librarian is a separate step rather than something you do inline.

title: AI Studio
text:
The four-rung ladder
The labs escalate deliberately. Building an agent in Week 2 produces an agent that generates confident nonsense you cannot evaluate; the first third of the course is spent learning to evaluate, which is what makes the agent worth building later.









Weeks
Rung
What you do
What it teaches




1–3
Grounded prompting
Load the shelf; make the model answer from it; catch it when it reconstructs a paper from memory.
Evaluation before generation.


4–7
Tool-calling
The model produces the WBS, the network, the estimates — then you write the code that checks its work.
The model proposes; the code adjudicates. Kills the plausible-Gantt-chart failure mode.


9–12
Skills and agents
Package a repeatable job — EVM reporter, risk-register maintainer, hostile reviewer — with a written spec and acceptance tests you wrote first.
Specification is the skill. Writing acceptance criteria for an agent is requirements engineering.


13–16
Agent in the loop
Your final project runs an agent that maintains a live artifact. The report says what it got wrong and how you caught it.
Governing an automated collaborator — the part no PM textbook covers yet.

title: AI Studio
text:
The weekly loop
Roughly 60–90 minutes per module, outside class.
1. TUTOR (diagnostic)  — 10 min — what do I already wrongly believe?
2. Read the module     — 20 min — notes + one primary source
3. TUTOR (voice)       — 20 min — one question at a time, no lecturing
4. Write something     — 15 min — a plan, an argument, a worked problem
5. EDITOR              — 10 min — attack what I wrote
6. ROOMMATE            —  5 min — where else does this structure appear?
7. TUTOR (retrieval)   —  5 min — mixed questions from all prior weeks
Steps 4 and 5 do the work. The Tutor finds gaps; producing something and having it attacked is what closes them. A loop that stops after step 3 feels productive and mostly isn’t.

title: AI Studio
text:
Course policy on AI
Summarised here, authoritative in the syllabus: label it, verify it, own it. Every quantitative result a model generates is submitted with the code or hand calculation that checks it — that check is graded. The midterm is the one place the tools are set aside, because the reasoning it tests is the reasoning you need when the tool is unavailable or wrong.

title: Final Project
text: Teams of four run a genuine project-management engagement with an outside organization across the semester. Not a case study, not a simulation: a real scope, a real sponsor, a real constraint you did not choose.

title: Final Project
text:
Why a partner organization
Everything difficult about this discipline comes from the parts you do not control. A classroom project has a scope you invented, a sponsor who is your instructor, and no cost of being wrong. A partner organization supplies what the exercise otherwise lacks — requirements that shift, a stakeholder whose interest conflicts with yours, and information you have to go and ask for.
The engagement is small on purpose. You are not being asked to deliver the project. You are being asked to manage a defined slice of it and to produce the artifacts that management requires.

title: Final Project
text:
Finding a partner






FP0 is due Friday 11 September — do not leave this late



A team without a confirmed partner by that date is assigned one from the instructor’s reserve list, and the reserve projects are less interesting than the ones you find yourselves.


What counts as a partner. Any organization outside this course with a real, bounded piece of work in the next three months: a local manufacturer, a campus unit, a non-profit, a research lab, a student organization with a budget, a startup, a family business. It does not need to be an engineering project.
What you need from them.

One named contact willing to spend roughly 30 minutes every other week with your team.
A bounded scope with a start and an end inside the semester.
Permission to describe the project in a report and a presentation — see confidentiality below.

Where to look. Your own employer or internship; a faculty member’s lab; NDSU facilities, events, or student affairs; the Fargo-Moorhead non-profit sector; a family or friend’s business. Ask early — the request is small and most organizations say yes.
If you cannot find one. Tell the instructor before 11 September rather than after. There is a reserve list. There is no penalty for using it; there is a penalty for silence.

title: Final Project
text:
Confidentiality and intellectual property
Some partners will share information they would not want published. Handle it properly:

Default to public. If nothing sensitive is involved, your report is a normal academic document.
If the partner asks for confidentiality, tell the instructor at FP0. Your report can be marked confidential, read only by the instructor, and excluded from any public archive. Your presentation can be given with figures anonymized.
Never sign anything on behalf of NDSU. If a partner asks your team to sign an NDA, stop and contact the instructor. Students may sign personally only after that conversation.
The partner owns their data. You own your analysis. Say so in writing, in an email, at the start — a two-sentence email now prevents an ugly conversation in December.

title: Final Project
text:
The AI requirement
From FP2 onward, one project artifact must be maintained by an agent you build — the schedule model, the risk register, or the status report. You choose which.
The final report includes a required section, roughly two pages:

What the agent maintained, and its specification — including the acceptance tests you wrote before you built it.
What it got wrong. Every agent that runs for six weeks gets something wrong. A report claiming otherwise is a report whose authors were not checking.
How you caught it — what control surfaced the error, and how long it took.
What you would put in place to govern this agent if the project ran for two years and a sponsor made decisions from its output.







Point 2 is graded generously and point 3 is graded strictly



Finding your agent’s error is not a failure of the work; it is the work. What loses marks is having no mechanism that would have caught it.

title: Final Project
text:
Final report structure
Roughly 3,000–4,000 words plus appendices. Sections in whatever order serves the argument, but all present:

The project, the partner, and what success meant to them — on which dimensions, per Week 1.
Delivery approach chosen, and the alternative rejected, with the reason — per Week 12.
Scope: charter and WBS, with what changed and why.
Schedule and cost: the baseline, the actuals, and where they diverged.
Risk: the register, and the risk that materialized or the one you were most wrong about.
The AI section, as above.
What you would do differently, ranked by expected effect rather than by convention.

IMSE 656 students additionally include a methods justification: the choice of delivery approach, estimating method, and control mechanism defended against the empirical literature, with citations to the source shelf.

title: Week 1 — What a project is, and why anyone needed a word for it
text:
The evidence

Flyvbjerg’s database (>16,000 projects): 0.5% come in on budget, on time, and with the promised benefits. 8.5% hit both budget and schedule. Cost overrun by category (mean): nuclear waste storage +238%, Olympic Games +157%, nuclear power +120%, IT +73%, rail/tunnels ≈ +39%, solar ≈ +1%.
Immediately complicate it. Chapman (2024, 2025, PMJ / IJPM) analysed 125 rail and 280 road projects in Denmark, Norway and Sweden, 2008–2022, and found them typically delivered “on cost, over time” — Swedish road projects showed typical cost overrun of 2.7%, rail a 1.8% underrun. Base rates are not universal constants; they are properties of a governance regime.

title: Week 1 — What a project is, and why anyone needed a word for it
text:
Check yourself

A vendor tells you 71% of software projects fail. What would you need to know before repeating that number?
Your project finished 20% over budget and the client renewed for three more years. Did it succeed?
Give me a project that was an efficiency success and a business failure. Now the reverse.
If the iron triangle is inadequate, why is it still on every slide deck in the industry?

title: Week 1 — What a project is, and why anyone needed a word for it
text:
Attack this claim

“Because 99.5% of large projects miss at least one of budget, schedule, or benefits, the discipline of project management has essentially failed.”

Have students attack it. Available lines: selection effects in the database; the counterfactual is unmeasured (how bad would they be without PM?); “benefits shortfall” depends on who wrote the business case; the Scandinavian data contradicts universality; the base rate mixes project types with wildly different uncertainty.

title: Week 1 — What a project is, and why anyone needed a word for it
text:
Somewhere else entirely
Cooking a dinner party vs. running a restaurant. The dinner party is a project — fixed date, unique menu, guests who will remember it. The restaurant is operations. Notice that a chef who runs a restaurant well can still fail at a dinner party, because the failure modes are different: the restaurant’s enemy is variance, the dinner party’s enemy is the thing you forgot to buy.

Why does the critical path change during execution even when nothing goes wrong?

title: Week 5 — Schedule I — networks, CPM, float
text:
Attack this claim

“Managing the critical path is the core of schedule management.”

Attack lines: near-critical paths carry most of the realized risk; the CP assumes deterministic durations, which is false; resource constraints (Week 6) can make a non-critical activity the real bottleneck; CPM has no mechanism for the fact that people expand work to fill available float (Parkinson).

title: Week 5 — Schedule I — networks, CPM, float
text:
Somewhere else entirely
Cooking Thanksgiving dinner. The turkey is the critical path. The cranberry sauce has enormous float. Every home cook knows intuitively that you start the turkey first and that a five-minute turkey delay is a five-minute dinner delay, while a five-minute cranberry delay is free — that’s total float without free float, discovered without a textbook.

title: Week 5 — Schedule I — networks, CPM, float
text:
Studio
Give the same network but with one duration hidden. Teams must determine what values of that duration would change the critical path. This converts CPM from arithmetic into sensitivity analysis in one step.

Insurance underwriting. An underwriter doesn’t estimate whether your house will burn; they price a portfolio using base rates and hold reserves against the distribution. Vocabulary discipline first

Reference-class forecasting

title: Week 10 — Risk, uncertainty, and behavioural bias
text:
The controversy

Love, Ika, Sing et al. (2019, TR Part A, two papers) analysed ≈HK$115bn (≈US$14bn) of Hong Kong transport projects and found 47% deviated from approved budget — with cases of both over- and under-estimation. They argue the planning fallacy is a false dichotomy (“error or lie”) that doesn’t survive contact with homogeneous data, and that optimism and pessimism bias coexist (Love et al., 2019, IEEE TEM: 43% of Hong Kong social infrastructure projects underran their contract award).
Chapman (2024 PMJ, 2025 IJPM): 125 rail and 280 road projects across Scandinavia, 2008–2022, delivered generally on cost; no evidence of optimism bias or strategic misrepresentation. He argues prior work suffers methodological weaknesses in data provenance.
Flyvbjerg (2018, World Development) replies on the specific Hiding Hand question: yes, benefit overruns outweigh cost overruns in about one fifth of projects — but 80% show no such behaviour, so the planning fallacy remains the better general account.
Ika & Pinto (2020, IEEE TEM) propose accommodating both — the “Fifth Hand.” The pedagogical payload: a field’s most-cited empirical claim is under sustained methodological attack, and students should be able to say what evidence would settle it. (Answer: homogeneous datasets with transparent provenance, consistent baseline definitions, and pre-registered analysis — which is what Chapman and Eliasson attempt.)

title: Week 10 — Risk, uncertainty, and behavioural bias
text:
Check yourself

What’s the difference between a risk and an issue? What changes when one becomes the other?
Your risk register has 40 items, all rated medium. What went wrong?
Reference-class forecasting requires a reference class. What do you do for a genuinely novel project — and is “genuinely novel” itself a bias?
Distinguish the two mechanisms that both produce underestimated costs. Which one does more analysis fix?

title: Week 10 — Risk, uncertainty, and behavioural bias
text:
Attack this claim

“Cost overruns are caused by optimism bias, so better forecasting techniques will fix them.”

Attack: if the cause is strategic (political), better technique changes nothing — the incentive to misrepresent is untouched; the Scandinavian data suggests governance regime dominates technique; Love’s data shows underruns exist, so the phenomenon isn’t unidirectional; “overrun” is measured against a baseline chosen by the same actors.

title: Week 10 — Risk, uncertainty, and behavioural bias
text:
Somewhere else entirely
Weather forecasting. Meteorologists moved from single-point predictions to probabilities (“70% chance of rain”) and the public learned to consume them. Project management still overwhelmingly communicates single-point dates. Ask the class what institutional change would be needed for a sponsor to accept “P80: 12 March” — the technical work is done; the communication norm is the blocker.

title: Week 10 — Risk, uncertainty, and behavioural bias
text:
Studio
Pre-mortem. “It is 18 months from now. The project has failed completely. Write the story of why.” Individually, silently, 8 minutes — then pool. Klein’s technique reliably surfaces risks that a P×I workshop misses, because it removes the social cost of predicting failure. Then have teams convert the stories into register entries with owners.
